AIRPORTS-CHARLOTTETOWN-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT ON NEW TERMINAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the House will not be surprised that I am bringing forward yet again the question of the provision of a modern, up to date airport at Charlottetown. I brought up the subject most recently on May 24 of this year, and on January 31 and December 17, 1976. Hansard will indicate frequent inquiries over many years to many ministers.
While I would not say that the airport question is the most important one facing our province, it nevertheless has the
June 7, 1977

highest priority and urgency and deserves and requires immediate action.
The basic problem is that the Department of Transport has not kept pace with the airlines serving our province. Eastern Provincial Airways, a most estimable firm, brought us into the jet age by providing direct, efficient service to Montreal. Later Air Canada, through its flights 654 and 655, linked Toronto and Ottawa to the cradle of Confederation. But while the airlines were in the jet age, the airport stayed in the prop age. The terminal is far too small, there are too few seats, there is a deficiency in many of the basic amenities which a modern airport requires.
Like its sister Atlantic provinces P.E.I. would prefer to strengthen its own economy rather than depend on what are sometimes unjustly, wrongly, and outrageously called handouts from Ottawa.
One of the logical and most promising areas of self help is in the realm of tourism. But if we cannot get the people into the province with a modicum of comfort and convenience, we cannot aid the expansion of the tourist industry.
Prince Edward Islanders are friendly people and we give a warm welcome to tourists who usually number about ten times our own population. But amiable though we may be, we do not care for standing on one another's insteps at the Charlottetown airport. On previous occasions I have indicated the number of chairs in the waiting room and compared this miniscule number to the seating capacity of any one of the planes serving the airport. I will not repeat that mathematical exercise today.
Since posting this question for adjournment proceedings- indeed, just a short while ago-I received a letter from the minister which I regard as good news indeed, and I am sure he will not mind my reading it.
In reply to the question you raised in the House on Tuesday, May 24, I am pleased to report that preliminary design work of the new ATB at Charlottetown has now been completed. During this stage, there has been continued close consultation and co-operation between provincial and Transport Canada officials, and the resultant design incorporates modern passenger processing facilities in an aesthetically attractive setting.
Final agreement with all airport users on cost recovery, consistent with Transport Canada policy, is expected to be reached in the next few weeks, and is the one outstanding pre-requisite before Treasury Board approval-in-principle for the development program is requested.
I repeat that that is good news indeed. Charitable and forgiving as I am, I will omit today my usual references to delays and procrastination, and congratulate the minister for his report of progress. I am delighted that a design combining aesthetic and efficient features has been arrived at. If no one else has a kind word today for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), I do not mind breaking the train of thought in this Chamber and speaking in candor and honesty and saying that in this regard he has done a fine job. I commend him for it. I can only say to the minister, through his parliamentary secretary or whoever replies to me, press on with dispatch. We islanders deserve action, not because we are virtuous-which of course we are-but because we have waited a long time. A
Adjournment Debate
new, adequate airport at Charlottetown will be a major contribution to the transport element in Atlantic Canada.
If I am the only one to say so in this Chamber today, I say that at least to me this is a great deal. I say "thank you" to the minister, and God speed in his final act to give us what we need so badly.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-MAXIMUM CLAIM RESIDENT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA CAN MAKE AGAINST UNITED STATES IN EVENT OF OIL SPILL
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-MAXIMUM CLAIM RESIDENT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA CAN MAKE AGAINST UNITED STATES IN EVENT OF OIL SPILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter arises as a result of a question that was asked of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) on June 2 last. The question was in two parts, the first dealing with the maximum amount of money that British Columbia residents would be able to claim under the law against the United States government in the event of an oil spill. The

June 7, 1977
Adjournment Debate
question was prompted by the decision of the Kitimat consortium to withdraw their application for a pipeline at Kitimat thereby leaving the waters of British Columbia at a much higher risk because of the expected increase in the volume of crude oil that would be carried from Alaska.
We have known for a long time that the Aleskya line will have a surplus; we have known for a long time that the United States will have to find a way fo bringing that surplus to market; we have known for a long time, in fact since the days of David Anderson, who was a Liberal member of this House from Victoria back in 1968, that the waters of British Columbia would be placed at very substantial risk as a result of this project. The warning of the risk has always been there and has always been high. Yet here we are today, some eight years later, debating exactly the same thing that the Liberal member, David Anderson, debated in this House such a long time ago. That is a condemnation of the government for failing to take a co-ordinated stand in regard to the use of the waters of British Columbia, and secondly, for acting as a dog in the manger and not providing any feasible alternative for the Americans to avoid the certainty of pollution. JVhen I say the certainty of pollution that is what I mean.
In spite of all the new radar systems that are available, in spite of the new Loran system, in spite of the $16 million that the government is presently spending in terms of water transport regulation in those waters, when a 50-mile an hour gale hits the Georgia Straits and a super tanker loses power, there will be a massive oil spill in spite of all the regulations. I am willing to concede that the United States has now developed very strict regulations for the use of its tankers. We are going to have the certainty of an oil spill in those straits, however, and our government will stand condemned when that occurs because it has had enough lead time year after year to have presented a positive proposal for carrying that oil to market.
I stress that the minister has had an opportunity to examine the whole question and I hope we will receive a specific answer on what the limits to claim are for British Columbia residents. It is not as though there were no feasible alternatives to carrying the U.S. oil to market without using the waters adjacent to British Columbia. A proposal has been made in this House by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) that Gray's Harbour should be developed as a port on the Pacific so that none of the interior waters need be used by tankers. That proposal was worthy of investigation by the government, but it did not see fit to do so.
We have the use of the port of Los Angeles to take the surplus Aleskya oil but the reason the United States is not using that port is that environmental groups in Los Angeles have more clout than our people, and have impressed the United States government about the environmental sensitivity of those waters. That is one of the reasons why they will not carry that oil to United States ports.
The pipeline for Alaskan oil should have been a feasible project, but the answer the minister gave me was that no application has been made to the National Energy Board. Surely the government can do more than that do see that we
[Mr. Leggatt.J
do not suffer massive oil pollution in British Columbia. Surely some leadership should be shown by the government.
Last but not least, the British Columbia government made a proposal for transporting Alaskan oil by rail. That proposal is still feasible. The original proposal was for taking oil from Prudhoe Bay, but the present proposal to take oil from Fairbanks is still feasible. You know, pipelines suck energy from one place but put nothing back for the residents. If we had built a pipeline on the prairies to carry wheat in John A. Macdonald's days, few people would now be living on the prairies. Therefore the question of the pipeline itself must be considered seriously.
The rail proposal was made back in 1973 and deserves serious study. Certainly we should have studied the proposals for alternate routes made by David Anderson and others in this House; we should have encouraged the Americans to consider them. Putting it simply, we should have shown leadership for developing with the United States a joint oil port. We may need it if we must bring oil across the Pacific, for one day we ourselves may run short of western oil. Surely the government could have sat down with its counterparts and said, "This interior channel route is entirely unacceptable to British Columbia. What can we do together to solve difficulties concerning the Juan de Fuca Islands, the American islands at risk, and our own islands?" We did not do that. We sat idly by and now are presented with a fait accompli in British Columbia. The federal government stands condemned for letting down the citizens of British Columbia and for not providing for the transport of Alaskan oil away from our waters.

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-MAXIMUM CLAIM RESIDENT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA CAN MAKE AGAINST UNITED STATES IN EVENT OF OIL SPILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first question raised by the hon. member concerns the claims that Canadian residents can make against the United States in the event of an oil spill.
Under the U.S. Trans-Alaska Pipeline Authorization Act, a fund of $100 million has been established for payment of claims for damages resulting from discharges of oil from these tankers, on a basis of strict liability without regard to fault. These remedies are expressly made available to residents of Canada.
A new bill has recently been introduced in the U.S. Congress which would supersede the liability and compensation provisions of the TAPA Act. This bill, the Comprehensive Oil Pollution Liability and Compensation Act, provides for an increased liability fund of $200 million, and some of the concerns expressed earlier by Canada have been taken into account in the drafting of the new legislation. Other concerns are under discussion between Canada and the U.S.A. while the draft legislation is under consideration by Congress.
The second question concerned negotiations with the United States on alternatives to the use of Cherry Point by oil tankers. A variety of port alternatives has been studied and preliminary conclusions reached by Canadian authorities. These studies
June 7, 1977

indicate that there are no sheltered harbours or anchorages between California and the Strait of Juan de Fuca which could be practically developed as terminals for tankers above 80,000 tons. Offshore facilities such as buoys appear to be ruled out by the difficult climate and ocean conditions in the area. These conclusions unfortunately appear to rule out Gray's Harbour and other similar options.
It is our understanding the SOHIO Long Beach proposal would supply only a few of the easternmost U.S. Northern Tier refineries with the crude oil they require. The project cannot, therefore, be viewed as a satisfactory full alternative to proposed northern routes.
Among the Puget Sound options, we have concluded that Port Angeles, although not strictly satisfactory from the Canadian point of view, would be a less hazardous location than Cherry Point for a major terminal. This conclusion is know to the United States government.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: DROUGHT-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES ON PROGRAMS FOR PUMPING WATER AND DRILLING WELLS
DROUGHT-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES ON PROGRAMS FOR PUMPING WATER AND DRILLING WELLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question raised during this adjournment debate relates to the question I raised on May 5 as reported in Hansard on pages 5304 and 5305, when I dealt with the drought in southern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan. In particular I raised the matter of surface water for livestock, and of domestic water requirements of rural communities and small towns in that area. I want to give the House a brief update, if I may call it that, on the western drought situation.
Over the past couple of weeks the news media and many individuals, not only in eastern or central Canada, but in parts of western Canada, have assumed that the drought is over. That is ridiculous. It is true we have had some generous rains. They have brought a happy ending to last month's drought in the west, but not across the whole drought area. I speak of that area taking a line from west of Bassano, Alberta, running into the foothills of the mountains and cutting across to Swift Current, Saskatchewan. South of that line we still have very serious drought conditions.
Most of this area has had less than two inches of rain, and some less than one inch. I live right in the centre of this area. What rain we have had has come in small local showers. There was no deeper suboil moisture to connect with these small, scanty rainfalls.
A week ago yesterday I flew from Calgary to Medicine Hat by Time Air in a light plane at low elevation. Over the next two days I drove over all of my range along the Alberta-Sas-katchewan border and northeast of Medicine Hat. That is a considerable area, covering not only my own range but a good many of my neighbours.
It is true that the limited rainfall did start our grass, but only start it. That was about three weeks ago. That grass has now stopped growing. It has that pasty yellowish-green colour that I know so well that precedes the stage of drought when the leaves start shrivelling up from lack of moisture.
Adjournment Debate
Our surface water situation continues to get slowly but definitely worse day by day, and this will continue throughout the summer. There was no rain run-off to help the water situation.
Many cattle producers are trucking water for their stock. Some have been doing this for up to two months. These conditions cover a large area across southern Alberta down to the American border and into southwestern Saskatchewan. I emphasize that it is very, very serious. The drought continues unabated in this area.
Following the statement in the House on May 6 by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the day after I raised this question, it was given good press coverage in the west. However, there have been few details, if any, since, especially details with regard to the well drilling and digging program and water pumping, both from wells and rivers.
The PFRA field office in Medicine Hat has had little, if any, policy instruction. The Alberta provincial assistance program has been much better publicized. Their pumps and pipelines are now available for action.
During my response to the minister's statement in this House I suggested that the minister give more emphasis to and have more publicity on this program and the need for open, regular public information on the total drought picture. There has been very little, if any, even after his Regina meeting when he met with his special action group-only a brief statement that the meeting was held. There has not been any substantial information. This suggests that the minister does not have anything to report. Either that or he feels that the drought is over. Surely he is better informed than that.
I urge the minister to authorize and indeed speed up the PFRA well program and the pumping program. He should allow special leeway for extra deep wells or wells which are likely to cost extra capital amounts, and include pumping. 1 am not certain, but I believe my suggestion with regard to the eligibility of dug or bored wells has been accepted. If that is the case I am most grateful and I thank the minister and his staff.
I have another serious suggestion, one which I hope will receive the same attention. The limitation of PFRA assistance to only one project a year has been relaxed, and two projects are now eligible. This is not enough. This is the time, under drought conditions, to carry out water conservation projects. It is time to get these things done, and the limitation to which I have referred should be removed completely so as to encourage more and more water storage and conservation projects. No cattle producers or grain farmers could possibly take advantage of such a special policy-the high cost of dirt moving will take care of that.
Will PFRA bring about some special water projects in the Suffield block on both sides of the river? Requests have been made for such assistance to include wells and river pumping up and over substantial river banks and distances. I hope serious attention will be given to this, soon.

June 7, 1977
Adjournment Debate
Will my request for special pasture allotment for sheep in the Suffield area be given consideration? Finally, I want to comment on the fact that the new director of PFRA was announced a week or so ago as being Dr. Harry Hill. I welcome his appointment. I understand he has impressive credentials. I do not know this gentleman very well but I am told he is not to take over until September 1. 1 suggest to the minister and to the parliamentary secretary that this is not early enough. He should be there now.

subtopic: DROUGHT-CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCES ON PROGRAMS FOR PUMPING WATER AND DRILLING WELLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member will understand that it will not be possible for me to answer many of the points he has raised. They are well taken, especially the one about the publicity given to the federal program which we have worked out with the western provinces. I will bring the other points the hon. member has raised to the attention of the minister.
The recent rains in the prairie provinces have done much to alleviate water and feed supply shortages in the west resulting from drought conditions. However, certain areas still requiring rain and water supplies remain a major concern.
After a recent meeting in Regina with the provincial ministers concerning the drought situation, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) announced that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) had received Treasury Board authority to enter into 50-50 cost-sharing agreements with the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta for two new assistance programs for rural communities and for farmers to assist them in drilling deep wells. These programs are in effect from April 1, 1977, to March 31, 1978. The total federal contribution could amount to some $2.7 million, with $1.2 million allotted to community wells and $1.5 million for the farm wells program. Assistance is availale to the three prairie provinces to finance deep wells and associated water pipelines for rural communities with a maximum federal contribution of $15,000 for each project.
The farm wells program is an extension of the existing PFRA program. It offers farmers a special incentive of up to $950 for drilling deep wells to a maximum of 440 feet. Wells, dugouts and stock watering dams have been eligible for up to $550 each, and irrigation schemes for up to $600. The maximum level of federal assistance is now $1,500. Both programs are to be administered by the PFRA administration and the Regina task force is working with the three prairie provinces to formalize agreements for the water supply program.
It is also a fact that in certain parts of the prairies no deep water is available and that the deep well assistance programs would not be suitable. Bored or dug wells are therefore to be included in the well-drilling assistance programs.
These water supply programs should provide a longer term solution to the prairie water supply problem. The pasture and winter feed supply situation is being monitored by the Regina task force, and farmers are being encouraged to produce feed from alternative sources, such as oats.
(Mr. Hargrave.]

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Forrestall:
That in the opinion of this House the government's transportation policies have failed to encourage the growth of strong regional economies, and, in particular, this House condemns the Minister of Transport's Atlantic provinces transportation policy and continues to reject his attitude towards western transportation problems.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad at least 20 members have shown up by 11 minutes after eight, but I was hoping that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) would be here since the debate is about transportation. I was also hoping that the mover of the motion in the official opposition would be here since it is his motion.
I want to resume the comments 1 was making when some hon. members gratefully called it six o'clock so I could not speak any longer. I was mentioning the potato growers in the Atlantic provinces whose problems are not new.
I can remember asking questions in the House in the fall of 1968 and the spring of 1969 about refrigerator cars and storage capacity for potato growers at the ports of Saint John and Halifax, so there is nothing new about the problem. The trouble is that we still have old line parties in the government and in the official opposition.
What I want to say is that in the port of Halifax one of the things that was presented to us most clearly, when we were there with the transport committee, from various and sundry users and operators of the port, was the desperate need for a fast move on the extension of the container facilities at the port of Halifax. We were told that if it does not happen fairly soon, the port of New York will steal some of the business which should rightly be ours. When the transport committee
June 7, 1977

was in the Atlantic provinces last week, we were told that this was to the detriment of the port of Saint John or anywhere else in the Atlantic provinces. I was hoping that the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) would have mentioned that in his remarks earlier this afternoon. No doubt some of his colleagues will speak late this evening to expand on that.
I want to repeat my contention which I have held over a number of years, particularly since the Minister of Transport was appointed after having been minister of justice and also in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, that in every year since those desperate days every move he has made was designed to put the users of transportation in this country in a position where they were no better off and, more likely, worse off than they had been. His proposals for changes in the Transportation Act return us to the 1890's. I have heard little objection to that from the official opposition who also believe in competition, commercial viability and profitability in transportation, even though governments of different political stripes from the extreme left to the extreme right, and of every stripe in between, in at least two dozen other countries in the world have thrown out those concepts two or three decades ago.
Our country must recognize our geography and our climate and provide a system of equalized or subsidized freight rates. It must make a deliberate decision that people and goods will move in the most efficient way, whether it be on the short haul, medium haul, or long haul.
The Atlantic Provinces Truckers' Association confirmed what I have long believed, namely, that the hauling of bulk heavy commodities for anything over 200 miles was wasteful and inefficient. The railroads admit that they cannot do a better job with heavy bulk commodities because they cannot bear the capital costs of our rights of way, trackage and roadbed and recover the costs from the users. There is nothing new about that. The fact of the matter is that every mode of transportation since before Confederation has been subsidized and has required investment from the public purse at the municipal, provincial and federal level. It has always been thus.
If we are not prepared to return to the toll roads of the early 1800's or late 1700's, to return to a system where only the rich can travel or only those who can afford the cost of moving goods and services can be in business, then surely the government and the minister must get away from the nineteeth century concepts on which they are trying to operate. In fact some members of the official opposition have faced up to this. Some remarks of their spokesmen today who quoted Transport 2,000 and the submission made to the Committee on Transport and Communications in the Atlantic provinces in recent weeks indicate that there might be some members in the official opposition who are prepared to forget about commercial viability and profitability in transportation.
The hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East spoke about the four Atlantic premiers being sucked in, and he did not like that phrase. I called it a con job. The four Atlantic premiers were either conned or they gave away the store in giving up
Transportation Policies
some statutory rate provisions in the Maritime Freight Rates Act or the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act in order to get $100 million for roads and $25 million for airports. That flies in the face of energy conservation, of the most economical and efficient use of transportation. They were conned rather than sucked in. I find it passing strange how anxious those four Atlantic premiers or their representatives were to accept this package from the Minister of Transport.
I submit that the people in the Atlantic provinces have been betrayed again. A benefit they had had for many years they gave away, for what? There is some kind of biblical phrase that perhaps the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) knows better, which refers to a mess of pottage. That would apply to these statutory rate provisions which the maritime premiers gave up. Now it lies in the hands of the Minister of Transport to select the commodities which might or might not receive the benefits that they would otherwise receive under the statutory provisions regarding freight transportation.
The Minister of Transport, in collusion with two Liberal and two Tory premiers in eastern Canada, has betrayed the people again, and will continue the discrimination against people and products because of where they happen to live or be located. There will be no change. When you put $100 million into some more highways in the Atlantic provinces, which are relatively short compared to those in northern Ontario and western Canada, you will increase the use of energy and the cost of transportation, most of which will be borne by the provincial and municipal governments. That is why I say that if the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East thinks he has been sucked in-I chose the word conned-the fact is that the Atlantic premiers gave away the store. They have been party to a perpetuation of a transportation system operated on principles that have been shown to be not some socialist dogma but that have been shown to be inadequate, insufficient, and incorrect in dozens of other countries.
The minister is accused in a recent publication-which I will not refer to because I might be out of order-as a man who has never admitted he was wrong on anything. I do not know if he would ever admit he is wrong on the time of day even if his watch were out. It is time the Minister of Transport just once admitted that commercial viability and competition in the major modes of transportation not only do not work but also perpetuate discrimination against people in the Atlantic region, on the prairies, and in the far north. There is no way a federal government or any province can justify, for example, a dozen eggs costing $4 on an Arctic island. That is unfair and unjust. It is unfair that it costs $1.80 for two quarts of milk in Yellowknife. Surely on essential things which everyone has to have-

June 7, 1977
Transportation Policies

I find it strange that the national government and the governments of ten provinces and two territories-so that includes all the political parties-are able to equalize the price of a bottle of whiskey. I am known as a fellow who enjoys the odd drink once a month.
The price of a bottle of whiskey at Yellowknife, Rankin Inlet and anywhere in Newfoundland, British Columbia or any other province is equalized, but when it comes to a quart of milk, a head of lettuce, a pound of tomatoes, a bag of flour, a tank of propane fuel, or a tank of heating oil, the principle of the user shall pay applies. My party and I contend that that is an indecent way to treat people in this country, and the governments of this country, of every province, or every territory, and in particular the Minister of Transport, are guilty of allowing this to continue. A system of equalized and/or subsidized freight rates which allows people a natural advantage in the production of agricultural products or mineral products whereby these products can be processed where they are found is just, decent, and fair.
Why is rapeseed processed in Toronto or Montreal? Not a bushel of it is grown there. Why can people not have fresh milk, fruit and vegetables in Labrador, in the Northwest Territories or in rural Saskatchewan for the same prices they can have them in downtown Regina or Toronto? The minister, his government and the official opposition should face up to the reality that no matter where you go in this world, competition in transportation does not work.
We should treat people fairly no matter where they live. If we are all part of this confederation, we should not charge $4 for a dozen eggs in northern Canada or $1.80 for two quarts of milk in Yellowknife. If we cannot do better under this kind of system, we should eliminate competition and profitability in transportation.
Who is going to pay for it?

The nation as a whole should share this cost. If hon. members do not mind this expression, it is called co-operation. It is even called co-operative federalism, or a co-operative commonwealth.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on this motion this evening dealing with a very important matter. Indeed, there are not many issues in Canada which give rise to so much emotion and so many political debates as transportation. I read once a paper referring to some research made on the political interventions of members from the Atlantic area since the beginning of Confederation up to 1971 which had shown that transportation was the matter more often discussed and dealt with by the members from the Atlantic area. Of course, in a country as big as Canada, it is normal that transportation would be constantly discussed.
I find it funny when I listen to hon. members such as the member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), who were shocked because a dozen eggs and a quart of milk are appar-
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
ently very costly in the north. Those people do not mention who should pay for transportation costs.
All of us, you dummy!

Mr. Speaker, I think that the hon. member could use expressions that are a bit more appropriate to Parliament than the ridiculous statement he has just made. I am simply asking who should pay for all those things. If I understand him correctly, he says that everyone should pay. I say that this is idealistic and that it is very well to suggest we should as much as possible in our society absorb all costs, taxes, transportation costs, the cost of living and the cost of basic necessities on the basis of the ability to pay.
However, Mr. Speaker, this distorts reality because, for instance, someone who settles in northern Canada does not have an income that is set on the basis of equality. His income is based on the market and if a worker in northern Canada has a recognized trade, he receives a higher income and receives certain benefits. It is quite unrealistic in my opinion to think that in a country like Canada it would be possible to equalize our transportation rates for products going to the north, for instance. I say this is an example of not very realistic interventions when I think of the contribution made this afternoon by the hon. member for Darmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall). I read with interest his statement before the Railway Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission when it was sitting in Halifax, and I read with interest the comments made in Moncton before this committee, which will be sitting in my constituency tomorrow.
It is quite ironical to see that those newspaper commentators and editorialists keep claiming that there is too much input on the part of the government in the economy and that this government should reduce its spendings. Hon. members opposite keep telling us that the government should reduce the number of instances when it takes action in economic matters. Those very same people are now telling us that railway passenger services between Halifax and Montreal should be maintained though they are obviously running at a deficit.
Actually, I have seen figures released no longer than six months ago showing that for each passenger travelling on the train from Halifax to Montreal, the Canadian taxpayer, through the federal treasury, has to pay some $40 on top of the price of the ticket. Mr. Speaker, these are the very same people who claim that railway passenger services should be developed despite the prevailing situation. In my opinion, this amounts to promoting a policy that would be utterly unrealistic and lacking any common sense. It is obviously necessary to maintain a railway service stretching between Halifax and Montreal and probably from Montreal to Vancouver. However, it should not be necessary to maintain two or three itineraries, as together they are not profitable. 1 think it is quite unreasonable to talk about stepping up operations in this field while it has been clearly demonstrated that this would not be profitable. I suggest it is right to say that the government should maintain a railway service but stating that this service
June 7, 1977

should be operated on a greater scale seems to me a policy that shows a lack of realism on the part of its proponents.
I should like to deal briefly with one aspect of transportation that touches my constituency in northern New Brunswick, and suggest to the minister that he consider the possibility of a local service as well as a service from northern New Brunswick to Montreal, and connections from there to western Canada, the United States and Europe. In my view northern New Brunswick at the present time could have a local air service. By this I mean a service which operates within the maritime provinces. We are not served as well as we could be between northern New Brunswick and Montreal. I believe this is due to the fact that there was never a rational plan for the development of airports; instead they were developed through ad hoc policies. I see the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) is incensed by the fact that some decisions were ad hoc. The fact is that in 1939 an air force base was built in Chatham. The government and the public had to recognize that as a fact, but Chatham was not the geographic centre to serve northern New Brunswick. It is one of the reasons why airports were not located where they could serve all northern New Brunswick, and another airport was built at Charlo.
I have been a member of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications for many years, as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) should know, and I intend to sit on it again before too long. The hon. member would do well to study the geography of the country and find out exactly where different communities are if he wants to be an expert on transportation.
Northern New Brunswick is not being as well served as it should. It is now being served by Eastern Provincial Airways with a jet service which goes Montreal-Charlo-Chatham and back to Montreal, six days a week, with only one flight per day each way-no morning or evening service. One reason the flight goes in the middle of the day is because at that time the Eastern Provincial Airways jet is not busy on more profitable routes. Because the airline has convinced the Canadian Transport Commission that this route should be eligible for subsidy, there has been no incentive to provide the kind of service that would pay for itself. There has been no encouragement to rationalize a system whereby there would be more frequent service and, at the same time as having the jet service to Montreal, have service to other points.
It seems to me that this is an example of where a subsidy given to a transportation service does not necessarily provide the most efficient and most complete service. In my view, if there were a system whereby the carrier-in this case EPA is the only one that has the possibility of providing the service-I would ask the minister to invite the Canadian Transport Commission to look at the situation and convince EPA that if they receive the subsidy they should provide the local air service to northern New Brunswick as well as to Montreal. By doing that they would improve access to Montreal.

In view of the fact that the taxpayer is investing in this service I think we should insist upon maximum efficiency and maximum service. As I explained earlier, they could make such a service economic if they would take passengers from northern New Brunswick with more frequent flights-two or three flights per day, in the morning and evening-and fly them to Montreal from Fredericton or from Moncton. I suppose if one has business in Halifax one must go. One could return home the same day.

Air Canada, with a $12 million hangar under construction here that it claims it doesn't need and isn't paying for is negotiating with Transair Ltd. to share the 80,000 square-foot facility, it has been learned.

Mr. Speaker, as has been mentioned this evening, we are debating a motion which 1 believe is one of the understatements of the year-
That in the opinion of this House the government's transportation policies have failed to encourage the growth of strong regional economies, and, in particular, this House condemns the Minister of Transport's Atlantic provinces transportation policy and continues to reject his attitude towards western transportation problems.
As I enter this discussion on transportation policy I cannot but think of the words used by the writer of a book entitled "Canada-A Story of Challenge." This historian, describing the nature of Canada and the way in which its geography tends to have a profound impact on the social and economic fabric of the nation, wrote:
Barriers such as the mountains and the shield exact a heavy price in scattering the population. They make for sectional divisions and high transportation charges. They weaken national unity and retard national development.
Four indictments are levelled in this quotation. First, these barriers make for sectional divisions: second, they weaken national unity; third, they retard national development; and fourth, they make for high transportation charges.
It is true that in western Canada unfair and discriminatory freight rates have contributed more to western alienation and a decline in national unity than even the questions of language and culture. However, I would not attribute these unfortunate effects to the physical factors maintained by the author of the book to which I referred. Rather, I attribute them to the policies, or lack of policies, enunciated and implemented by Liberal governments in past years. In the area of transport we have shuffled from one transportation mess, to use the words of a former minister, to another, and if political prophets are correct in their predictions we shall soon see the demise of yet another minister and the installation of a successor.
Even at this point there appears to be uncertainty regarding the implementation of a comprehensive national transportation policy. The rail system is important not only for the prairie region but for all Canada since the quality of the facilities put in place primarily for the prairie provinces have a very great effect upon the economy of British Columbia and, indeed, upon that of the whole nation. The failure to maintain an adequate standard of trackage across Canada, the failure to maintain adequate rolling stock, the failure of the companies to update their facilities, the decision to make huge investments in enterprises which have little or nothing to do with transport are a matter of great concern to those whose livelihood depends to a great extent on the movement of products to and from the areas in which they live.
My comments this evening will relate chiefly to my own province of British Columbia, and in particular to the agricultural sector. Although arable land in the province is extremely limited, my riding is one of the most important agricultural

areas and I wish to relate my remarks to the motion as it affects conditions there. As a background to what I have to say I should like to indicate the extent and value of the livestock and poultry sectors of the agricultural industry in British Columbia. Farm cash receipts are as follows: cattle, $66,696,000; calves, $6,055,000; hogs, $11,599,000; sheep and lambs, $789,000; dairy products, $103,157,000; poultry, $36,969,000; eggs, $34,496,000; other livestock, $9,107,000.
This indicates the extent of the livestock industry in my province and emphasizes the importance of the feed grain situation in the province of British Columbia. I do not have the Figures for 1976 here, but I have figures up to 1975. An analysis of the last three crop years shows that the feeding areas of the province, other than the Peace River district, consume about 480,000 tons of feed grains per year, of which 9 per cent is locally grown, 10 per cent is terminal elevator screenings, and 81 per cent is prairie grains and millfeeds of American corn.
Because of various situations which have developed, one being the matter of transportation, the increase of the importation of American corn is very, very clearly outlined. For instance in 1972 there were 14,400 tons imported, and in 1975 there were 73,600 tons imported. The increasing use of American corn is the result of a number of factors-the cost factor, transportation costs, and interruptions in transportation through strikes and other situations which are forcing people in British Columbia to depend more and more upon imports from the United States.
The industry was incensed when the government announced a reduction of $4 per ton on feed freight assistance to British Columbia. We appreciate the fact that this was restored when it was pointed out by the industry, the British Columbia Federation of Agriculture, the provincial government, members of parliament and others, that the basis upon which this decision was made was actually a false one. This was particularly important to the Fraser Valley, for 80 per cent of the subsidized grain was used mainly in the lower mainland of the province and in the poultry and dairy industries. 1 am indicating this to show the importance of adequate transportation as far as the agricultural economy of British Columbia is concerned.
I am stressing the input problems which are being faced by agricultural producers, rather than the marketing of their product. However, there are a great many problems which are militating against the development and maintenance of a viable agricultural economy in the province of British Columbia. I mentioned first the lower priority which is assigned to the feed grain industry. We all recognize the importance of our export industry, but we have to consider that producers in Canada are battling in order to develop an industry and to maintain an industry without which the nation would be very much the poorer. So, we think of the lower priority assigned the feed grain industry; the lower priority which is recognized by transportation companies in providing

transportation facilities; the unfair aspects of the block system, which has been set up mainly to assist in the export trade and which militates against the maintenance of adequate supplies of feed grains for the domestic producers in the province of British Columbia; and the inadequate provision of modern rail cars.
Hopper cars are used for the transport of grains for export, and we believe they should be used in the domestic feed grain industry as well because they are needed there. That indicates how much we are out of line in endeavouring to move our products from the west to the east, as against the movement of similar products from the east to the west. In view of the way that the House leader of the official opposition spoke today, I am seriously wondering just where the opposition is in the House. Of course with the type of leadership which they have to follow, whether it be the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), or the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark), or wherever it is he is from, there is no doubt hon. members opposite have a problem, but I am really distressed to see this situation develop at this point in Canadian history.
I should like to return to a more positive note-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You could not if you tried.

-and reiterate what the minister has done on behalf of the Atlantic area. He has sat down in a very sincere and serious way with the council of maritime premiers,
Transportation Policies
including the representative of the Newfoundland government, Mr. Morgan, and after many hours of debate and deliberation has arrived at a decision to provide in the order of $300 million worth of subsidies for transportation paid in the maritimes in 1976, whether it be rail transportation, air transportation, or what have you.
In addition, he has discussed freight rates and assistance to provincial ferries in the Atlantic provinces. I submit that he has made a positive contribution on behalf of a government which looks into the heart of a problem and comes up with a solution. In this way the government has assisted the Atlantic provinces to overcome their most serious transportation problems.
When I consider that the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), who is a maritimer and is supposed to know and understand the problems of Atlantic Canada and who is called the official critic on transportation for the official opposition, would have the mitigated gall-
Unmitigated gall.

-my friend, who is a member representing one of the western provinces, who has just interjected, as a matter of fact travelled with the transport committee to the Atlantic provinces this past week. I might inform members of the House that in spite of all that might be said about citizens of the Atlantic regions in this country, whether they be members of parliament or elected representatives at the municipal or provincial level, and despite all criticisms that have been expressed by people in the maritimes about not being heard, about being a voice crying in the wilderness, about not being able to bring their points of view forward- and this might be ironical or amusing-in the past week meetings have been held in St. Andrews, New Brunswick, and the CTC has conducted hearings with respect to the rail-passenger service in the maritime provinces. On top of that the government has carried out in good faith its undertaking made some time last year to visit the western provinces, particularly the port and harbour facilities in Vancouver, and we also made good our commitment to visit the east coast.
Indeed it is history now that the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications has just completed an in depth visit to St. John's, Newfoundland; Saint John, New Brunswick, and Halifax when the citizens of that area were given every opportunity to appear and make their voices, opinions and interventions heard before the standing committee on the question of transportation policies, transportation facilities and subsidies, as well as on any other question they might deem appropriate to bring before the committee. Indeed it was a most interesting and enlightening exercise in which I had the honor of participating as a member of the committee.
Tell them how they kicked Ottawa around.

The fact of the matter is that, discouraging as it was to hear some of the witnesses who appeared before us

June 7, 1977
Transportation Policies
say that they might have appreciated having had more time to present and prepare more briefs, if these people who are concerned with dry docks, shipbuilding, and transportation questions in general, as well as facilities for containerization, had been seriously involved in this business, they would have known that we had made a commitment last year to visit the east coast. Had they been more aware, they would have known that it was stated in the House, recorded in Hansard, and in the proceedings of the committee on Transport and Communications, that we fully intended to visit the east coast, to visit Newfoundland, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia to discuss these matters and to hear the views of these people. Similarly, the Canadian Transport Commission will be visiting Halifax and Fredericton on Friday, June 10. They will be in my riding of Restigouche and will come to the city of Campbellton to give an opportunity to the people there to express their views regarding the need for a future rail passenger service in eastern Canada.
. I ask you, what more can the government do? It is conducting meetings in the very areas where we are being criticized. It is meeting with the various associations and organizations concerned with transportation problems in the area. The Canadian Transport Commission, under the direction of the Hon. Edgar Benson, is conducting hearings this year with respect to the rail passenger service. Last year the CTC spent many months in the Atlantic provinces deliberating on the whole question of the air passenger service in that region. On top of that the government has expended $300 million in subsidies for transportation in the Atlantic area. In addition- and this is not promise but a fact

recently the Minister of Transport announced that $125 million would be spent right away to assist the different modes of transport in the east, such as rail, air, ferry, and bus transportation.
In spite of all these positive actions by the government we see before us today this most negative motion brought in by the official opposition stating that they condemn the minister's transportation policy in the Atlantic provinces. How can a member of parliament from the Atlantic area rise in the House and make such a statement, let alone carry the responsibility of being the official transportation critic of the official opposition? It is quite beyond me to understand that. It comes right down to what I have said recently-although one who supports our democratic system would be reluctant to say this-that we have no opposition at all. They show no creativity, no innovation, no new ideas.
This is not a tired opposition; it is no opposition. They do not refer to the positive actions of the government such as the $285 million or $300 million paid out in subsidies. They do not refer to the inquiries and studies being carried out by the CTC with respect to the rail passenger service. They will not comment about the inquiry that was carried out last year with respect to the air passenger service. All they do is make measly statements here about the lack of effectiveness of the coastguard, for example, when anyone who had the opportunity to take part in the visit of the transport committee to the Atlantic area recently would know that a substantial amount of the
[Mr. Harquail.)
taxpayers' money is being invested by the government in the Atlantic area to do the best job that can be done there.
Let me say a few words about the dedication of the MOT officials. You will not find another civil servant or federal government employee who is more dedicated than the employees of the MOT, whether we talk about the people who work in the Department of Transport or about employees of Crown corporations. To a man these are good Canadians, God fearing, hard working.
Hear, hear!

They contribute in a most positive way to the work of the department. Yet we have to sit here and listen to the negative approach of the opposition. They do not seem capable of at least acknowledging some of the positive moves of the government. Yet the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East in introducing the motion-

own position in the light of the motion which is before us tonight.
I do not think it makes good sense or good parliamentary procedure for the opposition to interrupt proceedings in this manner. 1 suggest to hon. members opposite that perhaps they should have more meetings of their own committees to decide what is really right for this country in terms of the approach they should take in this House, and in terms of assisting in some concrete and positive way to making a contribution to this parliament, rather than trying to ridicule the government the way they do. It is really sad when we have to tolerate this type of interference.
When we were in the maritime provinces I said throughout the hearings that we should support the maritime premiers. Indeed the premier of New Brunswick has made attempts to find a solution to the whole problem of air passenger service in the four Atlantic provinces. A solution was put forward to the air branch of the Canadian Transport Commission with respect to utilizing the Canadian built de Havilland Dash-7, a 50 passenger aircraft which could be used to provide daily service between the four Atlantic provinces.
That is not to mention the possibility of utilizing the twin Otter in a way which would provide rapid transportation between the various municipalities in the province of New Brunswick. This is something I have had occasion to speak about previously. This is something I advocate and support earnestly.
I thought you wanted to conserve energy.

We have to do that in every way possible. An hon. member opposite who is a member of the NDP interjects. Yes, I am for conservation of energy, and it certainly does not make sense to me, in view of the winters we are faced with, to talk about replacing rail service or air service with bus service.
I am completely convinced that in every area of each of the four Atlantic provinces air service is the solution we should be looking to because bus service really does not make much sense in terms of a logical approach to the very severe winters we have. I think there should be a very close study made of the cost of the utilization of energy with respect to operating buses as opposed to an efficient air passenger service which could provide a more effective pattern of service to the travelling public. I appreciate that an in depth study should be made with respect to the scheduling of flights so that we can have load factors which will offset the costs we are faced with in these days of high fuel costs.
I appreciate having this opportunity to set the record straight with regard to some of the drib-drab we have had to listen to from some of the previous speakers opposite.
Is that the same as cow plats?

Their remarks on what the government is doing have been negative. I do not care what kind of politics or dollars we are talking about; any time a government

announces $125 million to alleviate a transportation problem in the Atlantic provinces, it is a darned good step, and I certainly would not have any truck with an hon. member from the Atlantic provinces who would speak in any other way, when I consider the very dedicated and sincere efforts being made by the Minister of Transport on our behalf.
Hear, hear!

As you were saying?

Has the hon. member for Restigouche received a personal political assurance that any passenger service which might be rendered in the province of New Brunswick will go up the north shore? Is that the reason he talks the way he does?
We've got it anyway.

It was presumed in the Atlantic area that that was a meaningful trip, but if the hon. member has the assurance that the passenger service will in fact, by a predetermined policy of the government, continue to go up through the north shore of the province of New Brunswick, then he could, of course, speak as he did in his own constituency. helping some of his confreres who will be denuded of any passenger service by a predetermined judgment. It may be an exercise in futility for the Canadian Transport Commission to conduct any hearings whatsoever.
Mr. Speaker, I rise again on a point of order. I would like to set the record straight.
Order.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. This is a matter for debate, certainly not a point of order.

The hon. member has asked for some concrete proposals, and I will give him one. We should insist, as the hon. member for Restigouche has done, on behalf of the Atlantic area that the rights extended to eastern Canada under the BNA Act be exercised by a policy of the government and its minister. That has not been done. That is a constructive suggestion, and because that suggestion has not been accepted by the party which the hon. member opposite embraces, it becomes an item of criticism. Those rights should have been extended to the Atlantic area and eastern Quebec. Those areas have been conscientiously and intentionally denied those rights as a result of government policy, and the hon. member opposite is part of that government party.
It wasn't much different when the Tories were in.

With all due respect to the hon. member from that socialist party to my left, when a Conservative government was in power rail transportation rates made it possible to move lumber to east central Canada by rail. It left the agricultural industry in eastern Canada in a competitive position, to which we are entitled under the BNA Act, when we shipped to central Canada. That is what the policy of the Conservative party contained, and that is why the remark of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) is really out of order.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us examine a few individual instances and the policy of the government as it relates to them. I admit that the Atlantic area has under used the passenger service offered by the railroads, but we should look at the history of that service. I went to a little school in Wolfville called Acadia University, one of the best universities in Canada, if not the best.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The second best in North America.

Mr. Speaker, that is obviously a prejudiced remark and history will reveal the cause of the prejudice. When I took a passenger train home I found myself stopped in the middle of the night, about 2 a.m., having to wait six hours in an isolated station with no services available whatsoever for the passenger service operated by the CP to connect with the CN passenger service. We went from there to Moncton and waited anything up to six hours before we moved up to the

village of Juniper. It was an 18-hour trip. Had the government of that time been concerned for the people who used the passenger service there would have been a reasonable connection provided.
To proceed to more modern times, the government has-and I think intentionally-disrupted the mail service by taking it from the trains which gave overnight delivery from Ottawa to my community and provided revenue to passenger and express services as well. When the mail was removed from the passenger service it heralded the demise of that service. This is part of the structure. Maybe the hon. member for Restigouche is not aware of these things. At that time many applications were received for the cessation of the passenger service in eastern Canada. Of course it has been predetermined that it will go up the north shore and that the rest of the province of New Brunswick will go without.
Let us look now at the port facility in the city of Saint John. The Standing Committee on Transport and Communications held hearings throughout the Atlantic area. Of course the hon. member for Restigouche paid a little attention to that but did not follow it up. We were told that facilities for the movement of potatoes, which is important to the province, had been inadequate for years. The railroads have been allowed to abandon the principle of proper provision of equipment for the movement of perishables on the rails, not only in eastern Canada but in Kelowna, in Ontario, and in any part of Canada in which there are perishables to be shipped. I submit that that makes the government subject to criticism. It can buy 6,000 grain cars but it cannot manage the agricultural structure in regard to perishables. It has a particularly blind eye when it comes to Saint John.
Let us see what happened in Halifax. I do not remember seeing the hon. member for Restigouche there. We were told by the Prince Edward Island Potato Marketing Board that they could throw a cat through the cracks in the door. We were told that the facility was so poor that when using the available shed, one exporter had hired all the heating equipment that was for rent in the city of Halifax in order to keep his product warm in that port facility. When the shipment got to its destination he was not sure whether the potatoes had frozen in transit to the shed or had frozen in the shed in spite of all the heating equipment he had provided to keep them warm.
I am told that I should not criticize; that I should be constructive. But let us remember the BNA responsibility of government to eastern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces- then we will not be critical because we will not have to be. The reasonable obligation of government in the field of transportation will have been fulfilled if these responsibilities are faced.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I do not remember seeing the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) in St. John's, Newfoundland, and at some of the other meetings. If he is going to get into the semantics of who was at what meeting I think the record should show that he missed the bus that was provided for him in Halifax. I happen to have been there and I know about that.
